name: Peters anomaly
aliases: central corneal leukoma with iridocorneal adhesions

reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A form of anterior segment dysgenesis defined by a central corneal opacity (leukoma) with a defect in the underlying corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane
Iridocorneal or keratolenticular adhesions strand from the iris or lens to the back of the corneal opacity
Presents in the newborn with central corneal clouding, and may be unilateral or bilateral
Glaucoma is a frequent and important association, so intraocular pressure must be assessed and monitored
Peters-plus syndrome adds systemic features such as short stature, developmental delay and cleft lip or palate
Implicated developmental genes include PAX6, PITX2, FOXC1 and CYP1B1, reflecting overlap with other anterior segment dysgenesis disorders
Dense bilateral corneal opacity threatens vision through both media opacity and deprivation amblyopia
reference.pathophysiology: Peters anomaly is a developmental defect of the anterior segment arising from abnormal migration and differentiation of neural-crest-derived tissues that form the cornea, iris and anterior chamber angle. Failure of normal separation of the lens and iris from the developing cornea leaves a central defect in the corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane, producing a central opacity, and persistent adhesions between the iris or lens and the posterior cornea. Disruption of the same developmental structures frequently affects the drainage angle, predisposing to glaucoma. Mutations in transcription-factor and related developmental genes underlie many cases and account for the overlap with the broader anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital glaucoma with corneal oedema and clouding
Sclerocornea and other congenital corneal opacities
Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome within the anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum
Birth-related corneal injury with Descemet tears
additionalInvestigations: Examination under anaesthesia with slit-lamp assessment of the cornea and anterior segment
Intraocular pressure measurement and gonioscopy to detect glaucoma and angle anomalies
Anterior segment imaging or ultrasound biomicroscopy to define adhesions and lens position
Systemic and dysmorphology assessment for Peters-plus features
Molecular genetic testing of anterior segment dysgenesis genes where indicated
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure indicating associated glaucoma
Dense bilateral corneal opacity risking irreversible deprivation amblyopia
Progressive corneal decompensation or worsening opacity
Systemic features suggesting Peters-plus syndrome requiring paediatric evaluation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the density and laterality of the opacity and on glaucoma control; milder unilateral cases may retain useful vision, while dense bilateral disease has a guarded outlook even after corneal transplantation, which carries high rejection and complication rates in infants.
pitfalls: Failing to detect and treat associated glaucoma, a major cause of poor outcome
Overlooking amblyopia management alongside surgical treatment of the opacity
Assuming an isolated eye disorder and missing Peters-plus systemic features
Underestimating the difficulty and risks of paediatric corneal transplantation
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Prioritise amblyopia management with optical correction and occlusion therapy to maximise visual development
Detect and control glaucoma, escalating from medical therapy to surgery, with regular intraocular pressure monitoring

Consider penetrating keratoplasty or keratoprosthesis for dense or bilateral corneal opacity, accepting the high rejection and complication rates in infants, while optical iridectomy may suffice for milder cases
Examination under anaesthesia and regular ophthalmic review to guide the timing of intervention
Systemic and dysmorphology assessment for Peters-plus syndrome with broader paediatric input
Genetic counselling and molecular testing of anterior segment dysgenesis genes such as PAX6, PITX2, FOXC1 and CYP1B1
Low-vision support and coordinated paediatric ophthalmology follow-up
